content.title: About
content.content: A chicken drumstick is the lower part of the thigh, containing meat, skin, and a small bone. When sauteed, the skin becomes crisp while the meat stays juicy. The product is rich in protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as iron and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in many cuisines, from American BBQ to Asian stir‑fries.
Leaving the skin on during cooking adds flavor, texture, and beneficial fatty acids.
The "saute" method first sears the drumstick on high heat, then finishes it at a lower temperature for even cooking.
Drumsticks are easier to cook to a safe internal temperature than breast meat because of their higher fat content.
In some cultures, chicken drumsticks are considered a celebratory dish served at special occasions.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and riboflavin (B2), which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: Iron aids oxygen transport, while zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: The skin supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can be heart‑healthy when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Collagen content
items.content: Chicken skin is a source of collagen, which may benefit skin, joint, and connective‑tissue health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked drumsticks may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter. Cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: High sodium if salted
items.content: Added salt during cooking increases sodium intake, which can be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Although uncommon, some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: The skin contains saturated fat; frequent consumption should be balanced with overall dietary fat intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drumsticks can be sauteed in a little oil, baked, or braised in sauces. The skin is usually left on for flavor and crunch. Serve with vegetables, rice, potatoes, or salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Raw drumsticks keep in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked pieces can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for up to 3 months.
